# Lessons Learned

Written at the end of the project as an honest reflection on the experience.

---

## What This Project Taught Me

* **Real-World Log Correlation:** Before this project, "log correlation" was just a textbook term. Seeing how an interactive Nmap scan triggers thousands of raw Suricata network alerts, which Zeek captures as behavioral flows, and Wazuh aggregates into a single event dashboard completely changed how I look at visibility.
* **The Reality of Alert Fatigue:** Even in a small home lab environment, the sheer volume of data generated by standard monitoring is overwhelming. Building the local Llama 3 script taught me that automation isn't a luxury for a SOC—it is a functional necessity to filter out noise and surface actionable data.
* **Practical Defense in Depth:** I learned that no single tool is a silver bullet. If a signature engine (Suricata) misses a highly custom technique, a behavioral tool (Zeek) or an endpoint monitoring agent (Wazuh FIM) provides the critical safety nets required to catch the activity.

---

## What Was Harder Than Expected

* **Open-Source Compatibility Matrixing:** I expected open-source tools to plug-and-play easily. In reality, managing the licensing issues between proprietary distributions and open-source forks requires deep technical digging, selective package management, and meticulous configuration checking.
* **Resource Optimization on the Edge:** Running multi-engine network capture tools (Zeek and Suricata) alongside log shippers on a resource-constrained hardware sensor like a Raspberry Pi requires tight configuration hygiene. I had to learn to balance real-time tracking against CPU and memory throttling constraints.

---

## What Surprised Me

* **The Velocity of Automated Scans:** I was shocked by how quickly network scanners and automated scripts hammer exposed or target interfaces. A single directory brute-force check or port scan creates thousands of discrete events within seconds.
* **Local LLM Competency:** I was surprised by how effectively a lightweight, local 8B model can parse raw, messy JSON structures and generate highly contextual security briefs when provided with clean, structured log data.

---

## Mistakes I Made

* **The Multi-Process Conflict Trap:** During initial network baseline testing, I manually executed raw binary capture commands (`sudo zeek -i eth0`) while the automated system manager (`zeekctl`) was running in the background. This created an operational race condition that crashed the system engine and displaced active logs into my user home directory. I resolved it by cleanly killing the orphaned processes via kernel parameters and strictly adhering to the orchestration framework.
* **The Configuration Spacing & Licensing Loop:** I lost troubleshooting hours to an infinite crash loop on the Raspberry Pi sensor, caused by a minor indentation formatting error in a YAML file combined with an aggressive proprietary handshake loop in a standard agent binary. I fixed this by purging the commercial package, ensuring strict space-based formatting, and deploying the targeted open-source distribution binary.
* **Host vs. Container Memory Constraints:** I initially tried to boot the database components within Docker without modifying the host environment, causing immediate database container panics. I learned that heavy database structures require direct host kernel parameter modifications (`vm.max_map_count`), which taught me to audit the underlying operating system configurations before initializing application layers.

---

## What I Would Do Differently

* **Licensing Architecture Planning:** I would trace the precise codebases and licensing structures of all endpoint agents and backend systems *before* downloading installation scripts to avoid version conflicts entirely.
* **Strict Orchestration Boundaries:** I would rely exclusively on service management daemons (`systemctl`, `zeekctl`) from day one of debugging, rather than attempting direct interactive binary runs which risk destabilizing system log targets.

---

## What I Want to Learn Next

* **SOAR & Threat Intelligence Integration:** Integrating Shuffle SOAR and MISP into the pipeline to automate threat intelligence lookups and orchestrate incident response playbooks.
* **Enterprise Cloud SIEM Operations:** Migrating these engineering concepts into cloud architectures like Microsoft Sentinel or Elastic Cloud to understand how cloud telemetry collection scales compared to localized infrastructure.
* **Malware Analysis & Forensics:** Learning to extract and reverse-engineer malicious payloads captured within the isolated honeypot environment to map precise attacker intent.

---

## How This Changed My Understanding of Security

This project shifted my mindset from a passive "tools just work" perspective to an active security engineering focus. I realized that security operations center functionality isn't just about deploying tools; it is about building resilient data infrastructure, maintaining service continuity under resource limits, fixing broken pipelines, and creating precise automation scripts so a human analyst can focus on what actually matters.
